### Prerequisites

This game is a practice of the content taught in the previous text (<htcite0>), where we learned to move the decimal marker (⚫) along the track and to represent tenths, hundredths and other fractional families on the Soroban (算盤) and the Suanpan (算盤). We recommend studying that text before proceeding.

source.page: Decimals with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
### Writing numbers on the abacus

Recognizing the importance of practice exercises as a way to reinforce knowledge (<htcite0>), we present below a game that uses the same abacus board as the previous practices. The game draws a random number, and the task is to represent it on the abacus bead by bead — while the game teaches, step by step, how the number is written.

#### How the game works

When the page loads, the abacus is initialized with the first level and a random number is drawn. The decimal point (⚫) is fixed at the units column: the columns to its left are the integer families (units, tens, hundreds, thousands), and the columns to its right are the decimal families (tenths, hundredths, thousandths and so on).

Follow the instructions between the level badge and the "➡️ Next step" button: each one asks you to write a single digit in one column. When you complete the step correctly, the message "✅ Correct! Click 'Next step' to continue." appears at the bottom of the abacus. After the last digit, a final step asks you to check the whole number.

When you complete the calculation, you receive: "🎉🎉🎉 PERFECT! 🎉🎉🎉". You can repeat as many numbers as you want at the same level with "🎲 New number", and you can advance to the next level with "⭐ Next level".

#### The eight levels

The game starts with numbers like **x.0**: one digit in the units column and a zero in the tenths column. Then a level is added for each integer family up to the thousands, always keeping one decimal: **xx.0**, **xxx.0** and **xxxx.0**. From the fifth level on, the thousands stay and the decimal orders grow: two decimals (**xxxx.dd**), three (**xxxx.ddd**), four (**xxxx.dddd**) and five (**xxxx.ddddd**), until all nine columns of the abacus are used.

source.text: Costa, M., Cardoso, A. P., Lacerda, C., Lopes, A., & Gomes, C.
